title: 2  Course Syllabus
text:
3.1 Course Overview
This course introduces the mechanical behavior of structural elements subjected to common engineering loads. The focus lies on stress analysis, deformation, and stability of structural members.
The material forms the foundation for later courses in structural engineering, mechanical design, and aerospace structures.

title: 2  Course Syllabus
text:
3.2 Learning Objectives
After completing the course, students should be able to:

compute stresses and strains in structural members
analyze torsion in circular and thin-walled shafts
determine stresses in beams subjected to bending
compute beam deflections
evaluate the stability of columns and predict buckling loads

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.1 Learning Goals
After this section you should be able to:

define normal stress and normal strain
compute stress in an axially loaded member
understand the relationship between stress and strain
apply Hooke’s law

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.2 Axially Loaded Member
An axially loaded member is a structural element subjected to forces acting along its longitudinal axis.
Examples include:

tie rods
columns
truss members
bolts

The internal force in such a member is the axial force (N).

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.3 Definition: Normal Stress
The normal stress in a member is defined as the axial force divided by the cross-sectional area.
\[
\sigma = \frac{N}{A}
\]
where

(N) is the axial force
(A) is the cross-sectional area

A positive value corresponds to tension, while a negative value corresponds to compression.

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.4 Normal Strain
The normal strain measures the relative deformation of a member.
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}
\]
where

(L) is the original length
(L) is the change in length

Strain is dimensionless.

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.5 Hooke’s Law
For linear elastic materials, stress and strain are proportional.
\[
\sigma = E \varepsilon
\]
where

(E) is Young’s modulus.

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.6 Example
A steel bar with cross-sectional area
\[
A = 500 mm^2
\]
is subjected to a tensile force
\[
N = 40 kN
\]
The normal stress is
\[
\sigma = \frac{N}{A}
\]
\[
\sigma = \frac{40\,000}{500} = 80 MPa
\]

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.7 Warning
The formula
\[
\sigma = \frac{N}{A}
\]
is valid only when:

the load is uniformly distributed
the member is prismatic
the stress distribution is uniform

Near load application points, stress concentrations may occur.

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.8 Summary
For axially loaded members:
\[
\sigma = \frac{N}{A}
\]
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}
\]
\[
\sigma = E \varepsilon
\]
These relations form the basis for the analysis of axial deformation.

title: 4  Normal Stress and Strain
text:
5.9 Exercises

A rod with diameter (10 mm) is subjected to a tensile force of (15 kN). Compute the normal stress.
A bar with length (2 m) elongates by (1.5 mm). Determine the normal strain.

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

6.1 Learning Goals

crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.2 Deformation of a Uniform Bar
Consider a bar of length (L) subjected to an axial force (N).
From Hooke’s law
\[
\sigma = E \varepsilon
\]
and
\[
\sigma = \frac{N}{A}
\]
we obtain
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{N}{AE}
\]
Since
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}
\]
the axial deformation becomes
\[
\Delta L = \frac{N L}{A E}
\]
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.3 Main Result
The elongation of a prismatic bar under axial load is
\[
\Delta L = \frac{N L}{A E}
\]
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.4 Example
A steel rod has

length (L = 2 m)
cross-sectional area (A = 300 mm^2)
Young’s modulus (E = 210 GPa)

The applied tensile force is
\[
N = 30 kN
\]
The elongation becomes
\[
\Delta L = \frac{N L}{A E}
\]
Substituting the values in consistent units gives the change in length.
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.5 Members with Several Segments
If a member consists of multiple segments, the total deformation is the sum of the individual deformations.
\[
\Delta L = \sum_i \frac{N_i L_i}{A_i E_i}
\]
This principle follows from compatibility of deformations.
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.6 Warning
The formula
\[
\Delta L = \frac{N L}{A E}
\]
is valid only when:

the material is linear elastic
the cross section is constant
the axial force is constant along the member
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members
text:
6.7 Summary
Axial deformation of a bar is determined by
\[
\Delta L = \frac{N L}{A E}
\]
For multiple segments,
\[
\Delta L = \sum_i \frac{N_i L_i}{A_i E_i}
\]
These relations allow computation of elongation in axially loaded structural members.
crumbs: 5  Deformation of Axially Loaded Members

title: 7  Beam Deflection
text:
7.1 Learning Goals
After this section you should be able to:

title: 7  Beam Deflection
text:
understand the relation between bending moment and beam curvature

title: 7  Beam Deflection
text:
7.2 Governing Equation
For small deflections, the elastic curve of a beam is governed by
\[
E I \, w''(x) = M(x)
\]
where:

(E) is Young’s modulus
(I) is the second moment of area
(w(x)) is the transverse deflection
(M(x)) is the bending moment

title: 7  Beam Deflection
section: 7.3 Example: Cantilever Beam with End Load
text:
7.3 Example: Cantilever Beam with End Load
Consider a cantilever beam of length (L) with a vertical point load (P) at the free end.
The deflection curve is
\[
w(x) = \frac{P x^2}{6 E I} \left( 3L - x \right)
\]
The maximum deflection occurs at the free end, where (x = L):
\[
w_{\max} = \frac{P L^3}{3 E I}
\]

title: 7  Beam Deflection
text:
7.4 Interpretation
From the formula
\[
w_{\max} = \frac{P L^3}{3 E I}
\]
we see:

increasing the load (P) increases the deflection
increasing the beam length (L) strongly increases the deflection
increasing (E) reduces the deflection
increasing (I) reduces the deflection
